 📡 Network Spy 

 
 The premium, high-performance HTTP/HTTPS proxy and traffic analyzer built for the modern web. 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

---
[...]
**Network Spy** is a cross-platform Network Proxy and Traffic Analyzer built with **Tauri**, **Rust**, and **React**. It intercepts, decrypts, and analyzes your application's network traffic with a stunning, high-performance interface.
[...]
Network Spy operates as a **Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)** proxy. It sits between your application and the internet, intercepting traffic to provide deep visibility.
[...]
1. **Proxy Interception**: The app starts a high-performance Rust-based proxy server on your local machine.
2. **HTTPS Decryption**: By installing the optional **Network Spy Root CA**, the app can securely decrypt HTTPS traffic using industry-standard certificate pinning bypass techniques.
3. **Capture & Analyze**: Traffic is captured in real-time and passed through our specialized **Superpower Viewers** for automated decoding of GraphQL, LLM streams, Protobuf, and more.
4. **Local Forever**: All data is analyzed and stored locally in a high-speed SQLite database. No traffic ever leaves your machine.

 
 
 

---

items.title: Secure API Debugging Checklist with NetworkSpy | NetworkSpy
items.snippet:
Secure API Debugging Checklist with NetworkSpy | NetworkSpy
[...]
# Secure API Debugging Checklist with NetworkSpy
[...]
for debugging REST APIs securely with
[...]
, authentication,
[...]
, and NetworkSpy.
[...]
Debugging APIs should not mean abandoning security. The goal is to make the real HTTP exchange visible in a controlled development environment while keeping production habits strict. NetworkSpy helps by intercepting requests, showing headers and bodies, and making HTTPS traffic inspectable when you intentionally trust its local certificate authority.
[...]
Before debugging backend code, confirm that the request appears in NetworkSpy. If it does not, the issue may be routing, proxy configuration, DNS, TCP, TLS, certificate trust, certificate pinning, or a client that bypasses proxy settings.
[...]
Use HTTPS for real API traffic. For local inspection, trust NetworkSpy's local certificate authority only in environments where debugging is intended. Verify that the correct trust store is configured. Browser, OS, Android, iOS, Java, Node.js, and containers can all behave differently.
[...]
Look at the method and final URL first. Confirm the base URL, path variables, query parameters, and redirects. A staging host or duplicate query parameter can waste an afternoon.
[...]
NetworkSpy implements HTTP interception by capturing requests at the network boundary. For HTTPS development traffic, it uses a trusted local certificate authority to decrypt the HTTP layer inside the TLS tunnel. It then shows the request and response details that matter for REST debugging: method, URL, headers, body, status, response headers, payload, timing, and errors.
[...]
Builder of NetworkSpy, sharing practical notes on debugging APIs, modern app traffic, and AI workflows.

items.title: Root CA Certificates for HTTP Interceptors | NetworkSpy
items.snippet:
Root CA Certificates for HTTP Interceptors | NetworkSpy
[...]
Learn why HTTP interceptors use local root CA certificates, how trust stores affect HTTPS debugging, and how NetworkSpy uses certificate trust responsibly.
[...]
A root CA certificate is a trust anchor. When your development client trusts NetworkSpy's local CA, NetworkSpy can generate host-specific certificates for inspected HTTPS domains. The client accepts those certificates because they chain back to the local CA you intentionally trusted. NetworkSpy can then show the underlying HTTP request and response while maintaining encrypted connections on both sides of the interceptor.
[...]
This explains a common NetworkSpy setup issue: traffic from a browser appears, but traffic from a mobile app does not. The browser trusts the local CA, while the mobile app does not. Or the app trusts the CA but certificate pinning still rejects generated certificates. In that case, read certificate pinning and mobile API debugging.
[...]
NetworkSpy uses the local CA to generate certificates for HTTPS hosts you inspect during development. When a client sends a request through NetworkSpy, the interceptor presents a certificate for that host signed by the local CA. After successful TLS negotiation, NetworkSpy can decode and display the HTTP layer: method, URL, request headers, body, response status, response headers, timing, and payload.
[...]
NetworkSpy then establishes its own HTTPS connection to the upstream API and validates the upstream certificate. This is not the same as turning HTTPS off. It is controlled local TLS termination for debugging.
[...]
This is especially important in teams. A documented setup process is better than ad hoc certificate changes. Developers should know which devices trust NetworkSpy, which apps are debug builds, and how to remove trust if needed.
[...]
If HTTPS traffic is not visible in NetworkSpy, check proxy routing first. Then check whether the client trust store includes the NetworkSpy CA. Confirm the certificate is trusted for TLS, not merely downloaded. Compare browser and app behavior. Check for pinning. Inspect whether the request is using a different network stack. Once traffic appears, continue with HTTP headers, status codes, and timeouts and retries.
[...]
Builder of NetworkSpy, sharing practical notes on debugging APIs, modern app traffic, and AI workflows.
[...]
